questions.question: Which of the following compounds is the most reactive towards nucleophilic addition?

solution.key_concept: Reactivity towards nucleophilic addition falls as more, and larger, electron-releasing alkyl groups are attached to the carbonyl carbon.
steps: HCHO has no alkyl group. Its carbonyl carbon is the least hindered and the most electron-deficient.
$CH_3CHO$ has one alkyl group, so it is less reactive than HCHO.
The ketones $CH_3COCH_3$ and $C_2H_5COCH_3$ have two alkyl groups each, so they are less reactive still.
Order: HCHO > $CH_3CHO$ > $CH_3COCH_3$ > $C_2H_5COCH_3$.
solution.final_answer: Option (2): $HCHO$
solution.why_not_others: $CH_3CHO$ has one electron-releasing methyl group. Both ketones have two alkyl groups, which add steric hindrance and reduce the positive charge on the carbonyl carbon.
solution.common_trap: Thinking that a larger aldehyde or ketone is more reactive. More and bulkier alkyl groups lower the reactivity.
solution.time_saving_tip: Count the alkyl groups on the carbonyl carbon. The fewer there are, the more reactive the compound.

questions.question: Choose the correct decreasing order of reactivity towards nucleophilic addition for p-nitrobenzaldehyde (P), benzaldehyde (B), p-tolualdehyde (T) and p-methoxybenzaldehyde (M).

solution.key_concept: An electron-withdrawing group on the ring increases the electrophilicity of the carbonyl carbon. An electron-donating group decreases it.
steps: $-NO_2$ is electron-withdrawing, so P is the most reactive.
Benzaldehyde has no substituent and comes next.
$-CH_3$ is a weak electron donor, so T is less reactive than B.
$-OCH_3$ is a stronger electron donor, so M is the least reactive.
Order: P > B > T > M.
solution.final_answer: Option (3): P > B > T > M
solution.why_not_others: M > T > B > P is the exact reverse of the correct order. B > P > T > M ignores the activating effect of $-NO_2$. P > T > B > M wrongly treats $-CH_3$ as activating.
solution.common_trap: Treating every substituent as activating. Electron-donating groups such as $-CH_3$ and $-OCH_3$ reduce reactivity.
solution.time_saving_tip: Withdrawing groups raise reactivity and donating groups lower it. Unsubstituted benzaldehyde sits between them.

questions.question: Propanal is more reactive than benzaldehyde towards nucleophilic addition. The best explanation is that
options: the benzene ring donates electrons to the carbonyl group by resonance, reducing the electrophilicity of the carbonyl carbon in benzaldehyde
the benzene ring withdraws electrons from the carbonyl group, making benzaldehyde less polar
benzaldehyde has no α-hydrogen, so its carbonyl carbon cannot be attacked by nucleophiles
propanal has two electron-releasing alkyl groups on its carbonyl carbon

solution.key_concept: In aromatic aldehydes, resonance with the ring reduces the positive charge on the carbonyl carbon.
steps: The phenyl ring is conjugated with the C=O group.
Resonance donates electron density from the ring to the carbonyl group.
This lowers the partial positive charge on the carbonyl carbon, so benzaldehyde is less reactive than propanal.
solution.final_answer: Option (1): the benzene ring donates electrons to the carbonyl group by resonance, reducing the electrophilicity of the carbonyl carbon in benzaldehyde
solution.why_not_others: Option (2) gives the wrong direction of electron flow. Option (3) confuses α-H acidity with nucleophilic addition; the absence of α-H does not stop addition. Option (4) is false because propanal, an aldehyde, has only one alkyl group on its carbonyl carbon.
solution.common_trap: Linking the absence of α-H to low reactivity in nucleophilic addition.

questions.question: Given below are two statements: Assertion A and Reason R. Choose the correct answer.

statements.A: Acetaldehyde is more reactive than acetone towards nucleophilic addition.
statements.R: The methyl groups in acetone are electron-withdrawing and increase the positive charge on its carbonyl carbon.

options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

solution.key_concept: Alkyl groups are electron-releasing. They reduce the positive charge on the carbonyl carbon and also add steric hindrance.
steps: Acetaldehyde has one alkyl group and acetone has two, so A is true.
Methyl groups release electrons. They reduce, not increase, the positive charge on the carbonyl carbon, so R is false.
solution.final_answer: Option (3): A is true but R is false
solution.why_not_others: R reverses the electronic effect of alkyl groups. Every option that treats R as true is therefore wrong.
solution.common_trap: Confusing electron-releasing alkyl groups with electron-withdrawing groups.

questions.question: Given below are two statements. Choose the most appropriate answer.

statements.I: Di-tert-butyl ketone is more reactive than acetone towards nucleophilic addition because its bulky alkyl groups release more electrons.
statements.II: p-Tolualdehyde is less reactive than benzaldehyde towards nucleophilic addition because the $-CH_3$ group donates electrons to the ring.

options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

solution.key_concept: Bulky groups and electron-donating groups both lower carbonyl reactivity.
steps: Bulky tert-butyl groups hinder the approach of the nucleophile and also release electrons. Di-tert-butyl ketone is therefore very unreactive, so Statement I is incorrect.
$-CH_3$ is an electron-donating group, so p-tolualdehyde is less reactive than benzaldehyde. Statement II is correct.
solution.final_answer: Option (4): Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
solution.why_not_others: Statement I wrongly treats greater electron release as an increase in reactivity, and it ignores steric hindrance.
solution.common_trap: Thinking that more electron release makes the carbonyl carbon more reactive. It does the opposite.

questions.question: The reagent used in the Clemmensen reduction of a ketone to a hydrocarbon is
options: $NH_2NH_2$, then $KOH$ in ethylene glycol with heat

solution.key_concept: Clemmensen reduction converts C=O into $CH_2$ in an acidic medium.
steps: Clemmensen reduction uses zinc amalgam with conc. HCl.
It converts $>C=O$ into $>CH_2$.
solution.final_answer: Option (1): $Zn-Hg$ with conc. $HCl$
solution.why_not_others: Option (2) is the Wolff-Kishner reagent. $NaBH_4$ gives alcohols, not hydrocarbons. $H_2$ with $Pd/BaSO_4$ is not the Clemmensen reagent.
solution.common_trap: Interchanging the Clemmensen (acidic) and Wolff-Kishner (basic) reagents.
solution.time_saving_tip: Clemmensen and conc. HCl both fit the acidic medium.

questions.question: A ketone also contains a group that decomposes in acid but is stable in base. Which method is most suitable for converting its C=O group into $CH_2$ without affecting the other group?
options: Wolff-Kishner reduction with $NH_2NH_2$, then $KOH$ in ethylene glycol with heat

solution.key_concept: Choose the C=O to $CH_2$ method according to the acid or base sensitivity of the other groups.
steps: The product must contain $CH_2$, so a complete reduction is needed, not reduction to an alcohol.
The other group is acid-sensitive, so Clemmensen reduction (conc. HCl) cannot be used.
Wolff-Kishner reduction works in a basic medium, so it is suitable.
solution.final_answer: Option (3): Wolff-Kishner reduction with $NH_2NH_2$, then $KOH$ in ethylene glycol with heat
solution.why_not_others: Clemmensen reduction uses acid, which would destroy the acid-sensitive group. $NaBH_4$ and $LiAlH_4$ reduce a ketone only to a 2° alcohol.
solution.common_trap: Choosing $NaBH_4$ or $LiAlH_4$ for the C=O to $CH_2$ change. They stop at the alcohol stage.

questions.question: Pent-4-enal, $CH_2=CHCH_2CH_2CHO$, is treated with $NaBH_4$. The product is

solution.key_concept: $NaBH_4$ reduces aldehydes to 1° alcohols but does not reduce an isolated C=C bond.
steps: The $-CHO$ group is reduced to $-CH_2OH$.
The isolated C=C bond is not affected by $NaBH_4$.
Product: $CH_2=CHCH_2CH_2CH_2OH$, which is pent-4-en-1-ol.
solution.final_answer: Option (2): Pent-4-en-1-ol
solution.why_not_others: Pentan-1-ol would require reduction of the C=C bond as well. Pent-1-ene would come from a complete C=O to $CH_2$ reduction such as Clemmensen or Wolff-Kishner. Pent-4-enoic acid is an oxidation product, not a reduction product.
solution.common_trap: Assuming $NaBH_4$ also saturates the C=C bond.

questions.question: Match List-I with List-II and choose the correct answer.

list_I.label: D
list_I.text: Oxidation of an aldehyde with Tollens' reagent

solution.key_concept: Learn the medium and the product for each oxidation and reduction method.
steps: Clemmensen reduction uses $Zn-Hg$ and conc. HCl in an acidic medium: A-III.
Wolff-Kishner reduction goes through the hydrazone, then KOH in ethylene glycol, releasing $N_2$: B-I.
$NaBH_4$ reduces a ketone to a 2° alcohol: C-II.
Tollens' reagent oxidises an aldehyde to the acid: D-IV.
solution.final_answer: Option (1): A-III, B-I, C-II, D-IV
solution.why_not_others: The other matchings swap Clemmensen with Wolff-Kishner, swap the alcohol with the acid, or do both.
solution.common_trap: Interchanging the acidic and basic reduction methods.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about oxidation and reduction of carbonyl compounds are correct?

statements.A: Aldehydes are easily oxidised to carboxylic acids even by mild oxidising agents such as Tollens' reagent.
statements.B: Ketones are oxidised only under vigorous conditions, with C–C bond cleavage giving acids with fewer carbon atoms.
statements.D: Both Clemmensen and Wolff-Kishner reductions convert a C=O group into $CH_2$, giving a hydrocarbon.
statements.E: $NaBH_4$ reduces an isolated C=C bond along with the C=O group.

options: A, B, D and E only

solution.key_concept: Aldehydes are easily oxidised and ketones are not. Hydride reagents give alcohols, while Clemmensen and Wolff-Kishner reductions give hydrocarbons.
steps: A is true: mild agents oxidise aldehydes.
B is true: ketones need strong oxidants and undergo C–C cleavage.
C is false: ketones give 2° alcohols, not 1° alcohols.
D is true: both methods convert C=O into $CH_2$.
E is false: $NaBH_4$ does not reduce an isolated C=C bond.
solution.final_answer: Option (4): A, B and D only
solution.why_not_others: Every other option includes C or E, which are false, or leaves out a true statement.
solution.common_trap: Thinking that ketones give primary alcohols on reduction.
solution.time_saving_tip: Rule out C first. Every option containing C is then eliminated.

questions.question: Which of the following compounds has no α-hydrogen?

solution.key_concept: An α-carbon bearing three alkyl groups has no hydrogen.
steps: In $(CH_3)_3CCHO$, the carbon next to CHO is quaternary, so there is no α-H.
Each of the other compounds has at least one H on the α-carbon.
solution.final_answer: Option (1): $(CH_3)_3CCHO$
solution.why_not_others: $CH_3CHO$ has 3 α-H, $CH_3COCH_3$ has 6 α-H, and $(CH_3)_2CHCHO$ has 1 α-H on the isopropyl carbon.
solution.common_trap: Assuming an isopropyl α-carbon has no α-H. It still has one.

questions.question: Which of the following hydrogens is the most acidic?
options: A hydrogen of the $CH_2$ group in $CH_3COCH_2COCH_3$

solution.key_concept: A hydrogen flanked by two carbonyl groups is much more acidic ($pK_a$ about 9–11) than an ordinary α-H.
steps: Ethane hydrogens have $pK_a$ about 50.
Hydrogens α to a single C=O group, such as those in acetone, have $pK_a$ about 19–20.
The $CH_2$ group between the two C=O groups of a 1,3-dicarbonyl compound has $pK_a$ about 9–11, so it is the most acidic.
solution.final_answer: Option (2): A hydrogen of the $CH_2$ group in $CH_3COCH_2COCH_3$
solution.why_not_others: The terminal methyl hydrogens of $CH_3COCH_2COCH_3$ are α to only one C=O group, like those of acetone. Ethane has no carbonyl group at all.
solution.common_trap: Assuming every hydrogen in a 1,3-dicarbonyl compound is equally acidic.

questions.question: How many α-hydrogens are present in 2,2-dimethylpentan-3-one, $(CH_3)_3C-CO-CH_2CH_3$?

solution.key_concept: α-Hydrogens are only those attached directly to a carbon adjacent to the C=O group.
steps: One α-carbon is the tert-butyl carbon, which is quaternary and has 0 H.
The other α-carbon is the $CH_2$ of the ethyl group, which has 2 H.
Total α-H = 2.
solution.final_answer: Option (4): 2
solution.why_not_others: 11 counts the nine tert-butyl methyl hydrogens as α. 5 counts all the ethyl hydrogens. 3 counts the terminal $CH_3$ hydrogens, which are β.
solution.common_trap: Treating the methyl hydrogens of a tert-butyl group as α-hydrogens.

questions.question: Given below are two statements: Assertion A and Reason R. Choose the correct answer.

statements.A: Benzophenone, $C_6H_5COC_6H_5$, cannot form an enolate ion.
statements.R: A hydrogen lying between two carbonyl groups in a 1,3-dicarbonyl compound is more acidic than an α-hydrogen of acetone.

options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

solution.key_concept: Enolate formation requires an α-H. Two carbonyl groups increase α-H acidity.
steps: Both α-carbons of benzophenone are ring carbons that carry no H, so it has no α-H. A is true.
1,3-dicarbonyl compounds have $pK_a$ about 9–11, compared with about 19–20 for acetone. R is true.
A follows from the absence of α-H, not from the acidity of 1,3-dicarbonyl compounds. R does not explain A.
solution.final_answer: Option (2): Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
solution.why_not_others: Both statements are true, so options (3) and (4) are wrong. R does not explain A, so option (1) is wrong.
solution.common_trap: Choosing option (1) just because both statements concern α-H acidity.

questions.question: Given below are two statements. Choose the most appropriate answer.

statements.I: In 2,2-dimethylpropanal, $(CH_3)_3CCHO$, the α-carbon carries one hydrogen, so the compound undergoes aldol condensation with dilute NaOH.
statements.II: In the enolate ion of acetone, the negative charge is shared between the α-carbon and the oxygen atom by resonance.

options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

solution.key_concept: Enolate formation needs an α-H, and the enolate is stabilised by resonance.
steps: The α-carbon of $(CH_3)_3CCHO$ carries three methyl groups and no H. It cannot form an enolate, so it does not undergo aldol condensation. Statement I is incorrect.
In the enolate, the negative charge is delocalised between the α-carbon and the oxygen. Statement II is correct.
solution.final_answer: Option (4): Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
solution.why_not_others: Statement I miscounts the α-hydrogens.
solution.common_trap: Confusing tert-butyl (no α-H) with isopropyl (one α-H).

questions.question: Ethanal is treated with dilute NaOH and the product is then heated. The final organic product is

solution.key_concept: On heating, the aldol loses water to give an α,β-unsaturated aldehyde.
steps: Dilute NaOH gives the aldol, $CH_3CH(OH)CH_2CHO$.
Heating removes $H_2O$, giving $CH_3CH=CHCHO$, which is but-2-enal.
solution.final_answer: Option (1): But-2-enal
solution.why_not_others: 3-Hydroxybutanal is the product before heating. Ethanol and sodium ethanoate would be Cannizzaro-type products, which do not form because ethanal has α-H. Butanal is a saturated aldehyde and does not form.
solution.common_trap: Stopping at the aldol stage even though heating is specified.

questions.question: A mixture of formaldehyde and benzaldehyde is heated with concentrated NaOH. The main products are

solution.key_concept: In crossed Cannizzaro reaction, HCHO is always the molecule oxidised, to formate.
steps: Neither aldehyde has an α-H, so with conc. NaOH a Cannizzaro reaction occurs.
HCHO is oxidised to $HCOO^-$, which appears as sodium formate.
Benzaldehyde is reduced to $C_6H_5CH_2OH$.
solution.final_answer: Option (4): Sodium formate and benzyl alcohol
solution.why_not_others: Option (1) reverses which aldehyde is oxidised and which is reduced. Options (2) and (3) show both aldehydes reduced or both oxidised, which cannot happen in a disproportionation.
solution.common_trap: Assuming benzaldehyde is the molecule oxidised in crossed Cannizzaro.
solution.time_saving_tip: In crossed Cannizzaro, HCHO always becomes formate.

questions.question: Pentan-2-one, $CH_3COCH_2CH_2CH_3$, is treated with sodium hypoiodite (NaOI). Along with iodoform, the other product is

solution.key_concept: The haloform reaction gives $RCOO^-$ with one carbon fewer than the methyl ketone $RCOCH_3$.
steps: Here R = $CH_3CH_2CH_2-$.
$RCOCH_3 + 3NaOI \rightarrow RCOONa + CHI_3 + 2NaOH$.
The product $CH_3CH_2CH_2COONa$ is sodium butanoate.
solution.final_answer: Option (2): Sodium butanoate
solution.why_not_others: Sodium pentanoate keeps all five carbons. Sodium propanoate and sodium ethanoate remove too many carbons.
solution.common_trap: Forgetting that the carboxylate has one carbon fewer than the ketone.

questions.question: Match List-I with List-II and choose the correct answer.

list_I.label: D
list_I.text: Chloroform exposed to air and light

solution.key_concept: Aldol, Cannizzaro and haloform reactions, and the oxidation of chloroform, each give characteristic products.
steps: Ethanal with dilute NaOH gives the aldol 3-hydroxybutanal: A-III.
Benzaldehyde has no α-H, so conc. NaOH gives the Cannizzaro products benzyl alcohol and sodium benzoate: B-IV.
Acetone with NaOI gives iodoform and sodium acetate: C-I.
Chloroform in air and light gives phosgene and HCl: D-II.
solution.final_answer: Option (1): A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II
solution.why_not_others: The other matchings swap the aldol and Cannizzaro products, or swap the haloform and phosgene products.
solution.common_trap: Giving benzaldehyde aldol products, even though it has no α-H.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about aldol, Cannizzaro and haloform reactions are correct?

statements.A: Crossed aldol condensation between ethanal and propanal gives four products.
statements.B: In the Claisen-Schmidt condensation of benzaldehyde with acetone, the E (trans) isomer of the α,β-unsaturated ketone is favoured.
statements.C: The Cannizzaro reaction is a disproportionation that requires concentrated NaOH and an aldehyde without α-hydrogen.
statements.D: When pent-3-en-2-one, $CH_3CH=CHCOCH_3$, undergoes the haloform reaction with NaOCl, its C=C bond is also cleaved.
statements.E: Ethanol gives a negative iodoform test because it is not a carbonyl compound.

options: A, B, C and D only

solution.key_concept: Know the conditions and scope of aldol, Cannizzaro and haloform reactions.
steps: A is true: both aldehydes have α-H, so four crossed aldol products form.
B is true: the E alkene is favoured in Claisen-Schmidt condensation.
C is true: Cannizzaro needs conc. NaOH and no α-H, and is a disproportionation.
D is false: a C=C bond is not attacked in the haloform reaction.
E is false: ethanol gives a positive iodoform test.
solution.final_answer: Option (1): A, B and C only
solution.why_not_others: Every other option includes D or E, both of which are false.
solution.common_trap: Thinking that only methyl ketones give the iodoform test. Ethanol and $CH_3CH(OH)R$ alcohols also give it.
